analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to a regional $15 and ends the lower tipped wage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House floor vote; it sat in the Education and Labor Committee for the rest of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage gradually over two years, from 40% to 50% of the national average hourly wage for private-sector nonsupervisory workers, adjusted up or down for local living costs by region. In high-cost areas the wage would reach roughly $15 an hour or more; in lower-cost areas it would be set lower. It would also eliminate the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped workers and the lower subminimum wage for workers under 20 in their first 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly tens of millions of hourly workers, especially tipped restaurant workers whose separate lower minimum wage would end, and young workers who currently can legally be paid less. Workers in high-cost metro areas would see the largest raises because the wage is scaled to local prices.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to 40% of the national average hourly wage for private nonsupervisory workers in year one, 45% in year two, and 50% after two years, which at 2019 wage levels approached $12 an hour nationally and would keep rising every three years with average wages [S3].

Adjusts the wage for local cost of living, so workers in expensive metro areas like New York or San Francisco would earn up to 15% above the national figure, while lower-cost areas would get a proportionally smaller but still higher wage [S3].
Ends the tipped minimum wage, requiring employers to pay tipped employees the full minimum wage in cash rather than counting tips toward it [S2, S3].
Ends the subminimum wage that lets employers pay newly hired workers under 20 less than the minimum for their first months on the job [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers — restaurants, retail, hospitality, agriculture, and franchises — who would face higher payroll costs, with the steepest increases in low-cost regions where the wage would more than double in some places. Some employers would respond with price increases, reduced hours, or automation; economists debate how much.

drawbacks.text: Because the wage is scaled to regional prices, workers in low-cost rural areas and small towns would get a smaller raise than under a single flat national minimum wage, even though those areas include many of the poorest workers [S3].

Higher mandatory payroll costs fall hardest on small and independent restaurants and on employers in low-price regions, where the wage floor would rise steeply and quickly, and some businesses could respond by cutting hours or raising prices [S3].
Tying the minimum wage to average private wages creates a moving target: the floor rises automatically every three years even in a recession, when employers can least afford it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a substantial raise for the lowest-paid workers and the end of a two-tier tipped wage — is large and well documented as historically overdue, since the federal minimum had not risen since 2009. The cost is real but concentrated: higher labor bills for restaurants and other low-wage employers, and some risk of price increases or reduced hours. The regional cost-of-living design softens the shock for cheap regions but also means the poorest counties get the smallest raises, which is the bill's most serious design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Terri Sewell introduced the bill on April 4, 2019, with 12 Democratic cosponsors, several from competitive or moderate districts [S1, S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor that same day; no further action was ever taken on it [S5].

The House Democratic majority that Congress instead advanced a different minimum wage bill, the flat $15 Raise the Wage Act, which passed the House in July 2019; this regional version never received a markup or a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Restaurants and other employers of low-wage workers, including tipped-wage businesses, are better off because the bill died without a vote; workers in low-wage regions are worse off for the same reason.

for.name: Rep. Terri Sewell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on it

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, choosing instead to advance a competing flat $15 minimum wage bill that passed in July 2019

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, including moderates from swing districts, and no Republican publicly supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the tipped minimum wage, so these employers would have to pay servers the full regional minimum in cash instead of counting tips toward it — the single largest cost increase in the bill.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Their payroll costs would rise sharply, especially in low-price regions where the new floor would be far above current wages, and they could offset some of it through higher prices or reduced staffing.

industries.industry: Employers of teen and new hires
industries.note: The bill repeals the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, removing a discount on young labor.
